provisioning:The Lons markets.name: The Lons markets
provisioning:The Lons markets.teaser: Thursday on Place de Verdun for the food, Saturday on Cours Sully for a calmer restock
provisioning:The Lons markets.story: Shop Thursday's food market on Place de Verdun with a cool box and a seasonal list: a Mont d'Or now that it is back, cancoillotte in jars, fir honey, a Bleu de Gex, and a Saucisse de Morteau bought from the producer who smokes it. Ask for a hot slice with bread to eat on the move. Saturday's smaller food market on Cours Sully is for topping up.
provisioning:The Lons markets.why: Do the food stalls on Place de Verdun first: they pack up at midday while the goods stalls run on.

provisioning:Fromagerie Vagne.name: Fromagerie Vagne
provisioning:Fromagerie Vagne.teaser: Whole pieces of Comté cut to order under the arcades and sealed for the trip back to the boat
provisioning:Fromagerie Vagne.story: Here the galley buys cheese by the piece, not the slice. Ask for a wedge of each age of Comté you mean to serve, cut from the wheel and vacuum-packed so it travels without sweating, then a Morbier and, until spring, a boxed Mont d'Or to bake on board. For a big order, call in the day before.
provisioning:Fromagerie Vagne.why: Have the Comté vacuum-sealed in the shop: it keeps for weeks in the boat's fridge.

provisioning:Cancoillotte by the jar.name: Cancoillotte by the jar
provisioning:Cancoillotte by the jar.teaser: A runny, lean Franche-Comté cheese sold cold in pots: protected since May 2022, rare outside the region
provisioning:Cancoillotte by the jar.story: Cancoillotte looks like a pale, glossy custard behind the glass. It is made from metton, a dry skim-milk curd, melted down with water, butter and often garlic or white wine, and it stays runny once cold. Since 20 May 2022 the name has been an EU-protected IGP, and the trade sold the equivalent of about 25 million pots in 2024, almost all of them close to home. Buy the plain one and one with garlic, check the date, and keep it in the fridge on board.
provisioning:Cancoillotte by the jar.why: Buy a fresh jar from a market stall or fromager, not the supermarket tub, and warm it gently on board.
facts: Melted cheese from metton curd, under 15 % fat, sold in glass jars or tubs; IGP Cancoillotte since 20 May 2022
The Lons markets; Fromagerie Vagne; any fromager in the region
Warmed slowly and poured over boiled potatoes or a Morteau sausage, or eaten cold on toast

provisioning:Fort Saint-Antoine.name: Fort Saint-Antoine
provisioning:Fort Saint-Antoine.teaser: A frontier fort at 1,100 metres where Marcel Petite ages about 100,000 wheels of Comté
provisioning:Fort Saint-Antoine.story: The French army built the fort between 1879 and 1882 to guard the eastern border, half buried in the ridge between the Lac de Saint-Point and Métabief. From 1966 the affineur Marcel Petite turned its vaults into Comté cellars, and more than a million wheels have passed through since. Today a little over 100,000 sit on spruce boards in long stone galleries kept at around 6-9 °C. The air is cold and damp and smells of ammonia and toasted nuts. Visits are guided and by booking only.
provisioning:Fort Saint-Antoine.why: Book the guided tour, then buy a Fort Saint-Antoine wheel-cut to compare with the market Comté on board.
facts: Fort Saint-Antoine, 25160 Saint-Antoine, Doubs, near Pontarlier; in winter reach it only through the village of Saint-Antoine

provisioning:Volaille Miéral.name: Volaille Miéral
provisioning:Volaille Miéral.teaser: Four generations of Bresse poultry dealers in Montrevel, long the supplier of Paul Bocuse
provisioning:Volaille Miéral.story: In 1919 Claude Eugène Miéral took over the butter, egg, cheese and poultry business in Montrevel-en-Bresse where he worked. A century and four generations on, his great-grandsons Valéry and Florent run it, buying from around sixty partner farmers and picking each bird by hand. Gilles Pudlowski calls Jean-Claude Miéral the house's long-time supplier to Paul Bocuse at Collonges; Gault&Millau names Miéral as the source of a starred chef's poulardes. This is where to order the Bresse poularde for the galley: white feathers, blue feet, red comb.
provisioning:Volaille Miéral.why: Order a Bresse poularde or chapon ahead and collect it in Montrevel on the drive west.

walks:Lons at first light.name: Lons at first light
walks:Lons at first light.teaser: Under 146 stone arcades before the shutters go up, then out to the brine pool in the park
walks:Lons at first light.story: Start on Place de la Liberté under Bartholdi's statue while the cafés are still stacking chairs. Turn into rue du Commerce: about 350 metres of street carried on 146 stone arcades, rebuilt after the fire of 1637, the pavements still wet from the street sweeper. Number 24, with its plaque, is Rouget de Lisle's birth house. Branch off to the Romanesque church of Saint-Désiré, then walk on to the Parc des Bains and the Source Salée basin. Finish on Place du 11 Novembre as the Thursday traders set up. Wet stone, warm bread, then woodsmoke from the Morteau stalls.
walks:Lons at first light.why: The empty arcades in the first grey light, when your footsteps echo under the vaults.

walks:The cirque of Baume-les-Messieurs.name: The cirque of Baume-les-Messieurs
walks:The cirque of Baume-les-Messieurs.teaser: A Benedictine abbey under a horseshoe of cliffs, and the path up the cirque to the Dard's spring
walks:The cirque of Baume-les-Messieurs.story: The village sits where three blind valleys meet under a horseshoe of grey limestone. The abbey is first named in writing in 869; from here the abbot Berno left with a band of monks in 909 or 910 to found Cluny, a lineage the village still talks about. In the abbey church stands a 16th-century carved and painted Flemish altarpiece, one of the largest in Europe. From the village, follow the valley floor to the head of the cirque, where the Dard spills out of the cave mouth over moss and tufa steps. After rain, you hear it before you see it.
walks:The cirque of Baume-les-Messieurs.why: Walk to the tufa cascade at the cirque's head, then back for the Flemish altarpiece.

walks:The Hérisson falls.name: The Hérisson falls
walks:The Hérisson falls.teaser: Thirty-one drops in one wooded gorge, from the 65-metre Éventail to the Grand Saut
walks:The Hérisson falls.story: The Hérisson drops off the lake plateau in 31 successive falls, seven of them big enough to have names. The first is the Éventail, 65 metres of water fanning over stepped limestone, five minutes from the lower car park. Above it the path climbs through beech wood, behind spray and over wet roots, to the Grand Saut, a single 60-metre drop. In late autumn the water is high after rain, the trees are bare, and the gorge is loud and nearly empty. The paths turn icy once the frosts begin.
walks:The Hérisson falls.why: The Éventail from the footbridge below it, five minutes from the car, if you do nothing else.

walks:Belvédère des Quatre Lacs.name: Belvédère des Quatre Lacs
walks:Belvédère des Quatre Lacs.teaser: Four glacial lakes from one ledge, then the ridge to the Pic de l'Aigle and its view of the Alps
walks:Belvédère des Quatre Lacs.story: From the hamlet of La Fromagerie above Le Frasnois, a short path through the pines ends on a rock ledge, and four lakes lie below in a line: Ilay, Petit Maclu, Grand Maclu and Narlay, left in the hollows of the plateau by the last ice age. In late October the beech woods round them have turned copper, and the water is dark. Walkers with time go on along the ridge to the Pic de l'Aigle, just under 1,000 metres, where an orientation table names the Alps and, on a clear day, Mont Blanc.
walks:Belvédère des Quatre Lacs.why: The ledge itself, ten minutes' effort for the widest view on the plateau.

around:Poligny and the Maison du Comté.name: Poligny and the Maison du Comté
around:Poligny and the Maison du Comté.teaser: The cheese trade's own visitor centre at the entrance to Poligny, with a tasting at the end
around:Poligny and the Maison du Comté.story: Poligny, at the foot of the slope north of Lons, calls itself the capital of Comté, and the trade's own body, the CIGC, built its Maison du Comté here, opened in a new building at the entrance to the town on 19 May 2021. The visit goes from pasture to fruitière dairy to cellar, with the sound of a cowbell, the smell of warm whey and a wall of wheels, and ends at the tasting table with Comté at different ages. In 2026 it marks its fifth birthday with evening sessions. Afterwards, walk up into the old town to the collegiate church.
around:Poligny and the Maison du Comté.why: The tasting at the end, where the difference between a young and an old Comté is on one plate.

around:Salins-les-Bains.name: Salins-les-Bains
around:Salins-les-Bains.teaser: Fifty steps down to a medieval brine gallery where a wooden wheel still drives the pump
around:Salins-les-Bains.story: Salins drew salt from its brine wells from at least the 5th century, and the Grande Saline is what remains: a stone-vaulted gallery 165 metres long and 8 metres high, about fifty steps underground, kept at 12 °C all year. It linked the wells to one dug between 1224 and 1248. At its heart, a hydraulic wheel, a great wooden beam and the pump form a single machine 32 metres long, still working; you hear the water and the creak of timber. Since 2009 the site has shared a UNESCO listing with the Saline Royale at Arc-et-Senans, where its brine was piped.
around:Salins-les-Bains.why: The pump in motion in the underground gallery: medieval salt engineering, still working.
facts: By car north of Lons, beyond Poligny and Arbois
About an hour for the guided visit; half a day with the town

around:Dole.name: Dole
around:Dole.teaser: A tanner's house on the canal where Pasteur was born, under a 73-metre collegiate tower
around:Dole.story: Dole, the old capital of Franche-Comté, climbs from the Doubs to the Collégiale Notre-Dame, built from 1509 to 1574, its bell tower of 1596 rising 73 metres over the roofs. Below it, the Canal des Tanneurs runs between old tannery houses, water slapping at the stone footings. In one of them Louis Pasteur was born in 1822, the son of a tanner; the house is now a museum of his childhood and family. Note the calendar: the birthplace closed for the winter on 1 November 2026 and reopens in February.
around:Dole.why: The towpath along the Canal des Tanneurs, with the collegiate tower above the rooftops.
